buffer.title: When Colorado Closed Its Border to New Mexico - JSTOR Daily
buffer.author: @JSTOR_Daily
buffer.content:
The icon indicates free access to the linked research on JSTOR.

By the 1930s, the federal government was in charge of immigration, having centralized and formalized the ad hoc immigration regimes cities and states had developed during the nineteenth century. So it was news in April 1936, when Colorado Governor Edwin C. “Big Ed” Johnson declared martial law along the border with… the neighboring state of New Mexico. Johnson publicized his action as a blockade to stop a supposed “invasion” of “alien and indigent persons.”

When his earlier proposal to set up concentration camps for Mexican immigrant workers, who were pressing for higher wages in the sugar beet industry, came to naught, he hit upon the border blockade gambit. Political scientist Monica W. Varsanyi writes of Johnson’s “classic example of political entrepreneurship”:

Although his plans had little actual impact on Colorado’s agricultural labor market or welfare relief load, they resulted in an outpouring of public support, which he exploited in his successful run for the US Senate later in 1936.”

Beyond yet another precedent for the political benefits of racism and nativism, Johnson’s actions present a case study of racialization, the political and ideological process of race-making and the creation of color lines. The militarized race border between two US states, continues Varsanyi:

created circumstances in which the social boundary between who belonged and who fell outside of citizenship and belonging was both heightened and vigorously contested in this uniquely multi-ethnic region populated by Anglos, native-born Hispanics, Mexican immigrants, and Native Americans.

American citizenship had originally been granted to “free white” persons in the Naturalization Act of 1790. The territory conquered in the Mexican–American War added at least 80,000 people to the rolls of American citizenship in 1848. These Mexican Americans and their descendants therefore were considered white in federal law. But this was a precarious whiteness. In the Southwest, Mexican Americans were second-class citizens. Regardless of de jure law, Anglos did not see them as white and treated them accordingly. “Juan Crow” segregation covered housing, education, and employment.

Varsanyi quotes Colorado resident and US citizen Filigonio Arellano, “During wartime and when they need my vote, white people call me an American. If I need a loan, I am Spanish. And if I’m applying for a job they call me Mexican.”

Nonetheless, Johnson’s blockade received a good bit of support from native-born Hispanics. These US citizens tried to distinguish themselves as “Spanish Americans” or “Hispanos” in opposition to Mexicans. “Spanish-speaking New Mexicans, elite and impoverished alike, rebuffed claims of mestizo, ‘impure,’ or ‘mixed’ blood by tracing their lineage back to Europe and Spain, not Mexico.”

Birth of A National Immigration Policy

February 15, 2024

Until the Civil War, regulating immigration to the US was left to individual states. That changed with Emancipation and the legal end of slavery.

There was some “solidarity between Hispanic and Mexican workers, mainly within the labor movement and religious communities,” but otherwise little sense of a “pan ethnic/pan-Hispanic solidarity or ‘Mexicanness.’”

Of course, to a racist, birthplace or citizenship hardly mattered. New Mexico residents who were US citizens who tried going north for work in Colorado’s sugar beet, railroad, mining, and sheep-herding industries, as they had for decades, found that they were classified as “aliens” and “Mexicans” and turned back.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

The blockade only lasted eleven days. Pressure from the powerful sugar beet interests—who could not get white Coloradans to work under the industry’s brutal conditions—and rising tensions with New Mexico likely led Johnson to call it off. A marked increase in racism persisted long after, however.

Johnson himself would go on to serve three terms in the US Senate before becoming Colorado governor again in 1955. On both Wikipedia and the Colorado Virtual Library, only a single senatorial achievement is highlighted: on the floor of the US Senate in 1950, he denounced Hollywood star Ingrid Bergman as “a powerful influence for evil” and an “apostle of degradation” because of her extramarital affair with director Roberto Rossellini.

Resources

JSTOR is a digital library for scholars, researchers, and students. JSTOR Daily readers can access the original research behind our articles for free on JSTOR.

By: Monica W. Varsanyi

buffer.title: Cyberleek releases executable for GTA 6 Xbox build leaked last week: 'The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects'
buffer.author: Andy Chalk
buffer.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek appears to have followed through on their threat to release the executable of the Xbox build of GTA 6 they put into the wild last week, calling it "an early Christmas gift" for followers and explicitly linking the leak to efforts to recreate the game on PC: "The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects."

Cyberleek released a near-complete build of GTA 6 late last week, holding back only the main exe—the part that makes everything else run, basically—until either their crypto coin achieved a $15 million market cap, or November 23, whichever came first. The crypto missed badly, but time marches on, and so here we are.

The release of the exe, naturally, includes a call for more "donations" in its readme file (via Reddit) which Cyberleek said will go toward a secretive project "for the gamers." They also taunted Take-Two Interactive's efforts to track them down: "Months of takedowns, subpoenas and wallet tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving. No budget makes a lock unbreakable, and no court order deletes what the internet already has."

Leaks in the game industry aren't anything new, but this case is unique: GTA 6, effectively the biggest videogame of all time, still hasn't been announced for PC, as is Take-Two's way. But the advent of AI means the game could be emulated on our platform far more quickly than was possible in the past—some modders estimated it could happen within a week.

One of the leads on the Leonida recomp project predicted that things will start to move quickly from here:

At the same time, Shayder tempered expectations in a message on the Leonida Discord, saying "it will take at least a week" for the project to reach the point where GTA will be playable on PC.

How that unofficial emulated made-with-AI build would compare to the real deal is an open question, and I strongly suspect the answer will be "not well," but even just having something GTA 6-ish playable on PC is a headache that I'm pretty sure Take-Two would rather not have to deal with. I also wonder whether it will prompt Take-Two to release GTA 6 on PC more quickly than it has with previous releases. A rumor to that effect surfaced in October and I had serious doubts, but it's possible that ongoing emulation efforts will expedite its arrival..

The biggest gaming news, reviews and hardware deals

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I haven't verified whether the released exe is legit, but the previously-released material appears to be and the general consensus is that this is too. And with that, I will remind you (yes, again) that software piracy is illegal, and shady files from strangers on the internet can contain malware.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

She’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she said in a radio interview last year.

Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”

Talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.

What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

Game Changers

With the Golden State Valkyries shattering records in the W.N.B.A. last season, The New Yorker’s decision to put the Knicks on a recent cover is a missed opportunity (“Make It Two,” October 26th).

The Valkyries, in their inaugural season, in 2025, posted a 23–21 record and became the only W.N.B.A. team to reach the playoffs in its first year. In 2026, they improved to 32–12; earned the league’s No. 2 playoff seed; swept the defending champions in the semifinals; and advanced to the Finals. No expansion team has ever reached the Finals so quickly.

Their success extends beyond the scoreboard. The Valkyries have sold out all of their regular-season home games, averaging 18,064 fans per game—the same reported average attendance as their arena mates, the Warriors, during the 2025-26 N.B.A. season. With more than twelve thousand season-ticket holders and an apparent renewal rate exceeding ninety per cent for 2027, the popularity of the Valkyries is not a passing novelty but a testament to the growing cultural power of women’s sports.

Of course, the Knicks have a storied legacy. But why default to familiar heroes when history is being made before our eyes? The Valkyries are building a legacy in record time, and they deserve our attention. Give them their moment. Better yet, give them the cover.

Rebecca North
San Anselmo, Calif.

Too Big to Fail

I can’t help but feel that Justin Chang’s review of Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s “La Bola Negra” misses the point of the film (The Current Cinema, November 3rd). Chang rightfully traces the film’s queer art-house DNA, but there’s another touchstone: “Titanic” (1997). Ambrossi and Calvo have made this comparison, albeit jokingly, and a character in the film even pays homage to old Rose: “The heart of a faggot is an ocean full of secrets.”

Viewed through this lens, the monumentality of “La Bola Negra” makes far more sense. What Chang sees as a failure to fully realize the movie’s characters I see as a distinct way to bring them to life. The film pushes us to feel the characters’ longing instead of trying to rationalize it. No one asks that Jack’s psychology justify his self-sacrificing love for Rose; we simply understand his affection. So why should the character Sebastián need any more explanation to trumpet “his agony to the skies”? He has no choice but to do so, because the world in which he exists won’t allow him to express his anguish in any other way.

The film invites us to experience queer love on an epic scale. And, frankly, if the straights can have “Titanic,” why can’t the gays have “La Bola Negra”?

Michael Filocamo
London, England

Ahead of the Curve

Rivka Galchen, in her piece on A.I. and mathematics, explains that math is perceived as often “leading to all sorts of unexpected applications, like public-key cryptography and G.P.S.” (“Proof of Concept,” November 9th). But the mathematician John Urschel, Galchen writes, insists that instrumental justifications of math have “never been true.” His assertion conflates two claims about such justifications: that they don’t motivate mathematicians, and that they aren’t in the interest of the general public. The former is correct. The latter is not.

The returns on fundamental research are heavy-tailed: most ventures produce nothing practical, but the few that do pay for the enterprise many times over. The applications Galchen mentions are textbook examples. Number theory, which underlies cryptography, was famously praised for its uselessness by G. H. Hardy. Bernhard Riemann developed the geometry upon which G.P.S. rests decades before general relativity pointed toward any practical use for his work.

Revolutionary advancements depend on the willingness of researchers to investigate fundamental structures—suggested by, but often abstracted significantly from, tangible phenomena—for the wholly quixotic reasons Urschel describes, because problems chosen for foreseeable uses yield only foreseeable uses. With funding hanging in the balance, and A.I. creating increasing pressure against it, it’s critical to emphasize this.

Mihir Goyal
Singapore

The Good Fight

“The next Congress will succeed not through an obsession with retribution and punishment but by delivering on the myriad hopes and demands of the voters who elected its members,” David Remnick writes, in his recent Comment (November 16th). Congress must certainly deliver on the hopes of voters, but accountability is not retribution, and enforcing the law isn’t incompatible with improving people’s lives.

Calls to turn the page run the risk of enabling impunity. President Barack Obama’s decision, upon his election, to “look forward” rather than to launch an investigation into the potential wrongdoings of the George W. Bush Administration set a troubling precedent and probably contributed to the resurgence of the Republican Party in 2010, 2016, and 2024.

Congress can pursue a constructive agenda while still examining abuses and insuring that individuals and institutions are brought to justice. Upholding the rule of law would itself be a positive change, and one that voters have every reason to demand.

Donald A. Smith
Mercer Island, Wash.

•

Letters should be sent with the writer’s name, address, and daytime phone number via e-mail to themail@newyorker.com. Letters may be edited for length and clarity, and may be published in any medium. We regret that owing to the volume of correspondence we cannot reply to every letter.
